q: What happens to existing objects when you enable S3 Replication (CRR/SRR) on a bucket?

opts.a: All existing objects are automatically replicated
opts.b: Only new objects uploaded after enabling replication are replicated
opts.c: Only objects larger than 5 MB are replicated
opts.d: All objects including delete markers are replicated immediately

exp.a: Incorrect. Existing objects are NOT automatically replicated. You must use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects.
exp.b: Correct. By default, only new objects uploaded after enabling replication are replicated. Use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects.
exp.c: Incorrect. Object size does not determine eligibility for replication.
exp.d: Incorrect. Delete markers are not replicated by default (optional setting), and existing objects are not replicated.

q: In S3 Replication, are delete markers replicated by default?

opts.b: No, but you can optionally enable delete marker replication
opts.d: Only if MFA Delete is enabled

exp.a: Incorrect. Delete markers are NOT replicated by default.
exp.b: Correct. Delete marker replication is disabled by default but can be optionally enabled in the replication configuration.
exp.c: Incorrect. This setting applies to both CRR and SRR.
exp.d: Incorrect. MFA Delete is unrelated to delete marker replication.

q: In S3 Replication, are deletions with a specific version ID replicated to the destination bucket?

opts.a: Yes, permanent deletions are always replicated
opts.b: No, permanent deletions (with version ID) are never replicated to prevent malicious deletes
opts.c: Only if the bucket policy allows it

exp.a: Incorrect. Permanent deletions specifying a version ID are never replicated.
exp.b: Correct. Deletions with a specific version ID are NOT replicated. This is by design to protect against malicious or accidental permanent deletions propagating.
exp.c: Incorrect. This behavior is hardcoded and cannot be changed via bucket policy.
exp.d: Incorrect. Compliance mode is related to Object Lock, not replication of deletions.

q: What is S3 Replication Time Control (RTC)?

opts.a: A feature that schedules replication to occur only at night
opts.b: A feature that guarantees 99.99% of objects are replicated within 15 minutes
opts.c: A feature that delays replication by a configurable time
opts.d: A feature that replicates only during off-peak hours

exp.a: Incorrect. RTC does not schedule replication for specific times.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) provides an SLA that 99.99% of new objects are replicated within 15 minutes.
exp.c: Incorrect. RTC ensures faster replication, not delayed replication.
exp.d: Incorrect. RTC aims for continuous fast replication, not off-peak only.

q: Can S3 Replication be chained (bucket A → bucket B → bucket C)?

opts.b: No, there is no chaining. Objects replicated to B are not automatically replicated to C
opts.d: Only in the same AWS Region

exp.a: Incorrect. S3 does not support automatic replication chaining.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Replication does NOT support chaining. If A replicates to B, and B replicates to C, objects that arrive at B via replication will NOT automatically replicate to C.
exp.c: Incorrect. Batch Replication handles existing objects, not chaining.
exp.d: Incorrect. Chaining is not supported regardless of region.

q: Which S3 feature can be used to require that all objects uploaded to a bucket are encrypted with a specific encryption method?

opts.b: Default encryption setting combined with a bucket policy denying unencrypted uploads

exp.a: Incorrect. ACLs manage access permissions, not encryption enforcement.
exp.b: Correct. You can set a default encryption and create a bucket policy with a Condition that denies PutObject requests lacking the required encryption header (e.g., x-amz-server-side-encryption).
exp.c: Incorrect. Versioning manages object versions, not encryption.
exp.d: Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads, not encryption enforcement.

q: What is the maximum number of tags that can be assigned to a single S3 object?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can assign more than 5 tags.
exp.b: Correct. Each S3 object can have up to 10 user-defined tags.
exp.c: Incorrect. 50 tags is the limit for many other AWS resources, but S3 objects have a limit of 10.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a hard limit of 10 tags per S3 object.

q: What is the maximum size of an S3 object tag key?

opts.b: 128 Unicode characters

exp.a: Incorrect. The maximum key length is larger than 64 characters.
exp.b: Correct. S3 object tag keys can be up to 128 Unicode characters.
exp.c: Incorrect. 256 characters is the maximum for tag values, not keys.
exp.d: Incorrect. 512 exceeds the limit for both keys and values.

q: What is the maximum size of an S3 object tag value?

opts.b: 256 Unicode characters

exp.a: Incorrect. 128 characters is the maximum for tag keys.
exp.b: Correct. S3 object tag values can be up to 256 Unicode characters.
exp.c: Incorrect. The limit is 256, not 512.
exp.d: Incorrect. The limit is 256, not 1024.

q: What is the minimum part size for S3 Multipart Upload (except the last part)?

opts.b: 5 MB

exp.a: Incorrect. The minimum is 5 MB, not 1 MB.
exp.b: Correct. The minimum part size for multipart upload is 5 MB (except the last part which can be smaller).
exp.c: Incorrect. 10 MB is above the minimum.
exp.d: Incorrect. 16 MB exceeds the minimum requirement.

q: What is the maximum part size for S3 Multipart Upload?

opts.b: 512 MB

exp.a: Incorrect. Parts can be larger than 100 MB.
exp.b: Incorrect. Parts can be larger than 512 MB.
exp.c: Correct. Each part in a multipart upload can be up to 5 GB.
exp.d: Incorrect. 5 TB is the maximum object size, not part size.

q: When using SSE-KMS with S3, which KMS limit might you encounter with high request volumes?

opts.b: KMS request quota (GenerateDataKey/Decrypt API calls throttling)

exp.a: Incorrect. S3 storage is virtually unlimited.
exp.b: Correct. Each S3 GET/PUT with SSE-KMS calls KMS APIs (GenerateDataKey for upload, Decrypt for download). KMS has request quotas (5,500-30,000 per second depending on region) that can be a bottleneck at high volumes.
exp.c: Incorrect. IAM policy size is unrelated to KMS throttling.
exp.d: Incorrect. CloudTrail log size does not affect S3/KMS operations.

q: What is the default KMS request quota per second in most AWS regions?

opts.b: 5,500 requests/second

exp.a: Incorrect. The default is higher than 1,000.
exp.b: Correct. The default KMS request quota is 5,500 requests per second in most regions (some regions support up to 30,000).
exp.c: Incorrect. 10,000 is not the default for most regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. 100,000 far exceeds the KMS quota.

q: Which S3 feature allows you to restrict access so that objects can only be accessed through CloudFront and not directly from the S3 URL?

opts.a: S3 Bucket Policy with IP restriction
opts.b: Origin Access Control (OAC) / Origin Access Identity (OAI)

exp.a: Incorrect. IP restriction in bucket policy could work partially but is not the recommended method.
exp.b: Correct. Origin Access Control (OAC) or the legacy Origin Access Identity (OAI) restricts direct S3 access and ensures users can only access content through CloudFront.
exp.c: Incorrect. CORS handles cross-origin browser requests, not access restriction.
exp.d: Incorrect. Block Public Access prevents public access but doesn't specifically enforce CloudFront-only access.

q: What is the difference between Origin Access Identity (OAI) and Origin Access Control (OAC) for CloudFront with S3?

opts.a: OAI is newer and supports SSE-KMS; OAC is legacy
opts.b: OAC is the newer recommended approach that supports SSE-KMS, S3 in all regions, and fine-grained permissions; OAI is legacy
opts.d: OAC only works with S3 website endpoints

exp.a: Incorrect. OAI is legacy; OAC is newer.
exp.b: Correct. OAC is the newer, recommended method that supports SSE-KMS encryption, all S3 regions, and provides more granular security. OAI is legacy.
exp.c: Incorrect. OAC has more features and is recommended over OAI.
exp.d: Incorrect. OAC works with S3 REST API endpoints, not website endpoints.

q: What is S3 Glacier Vault Lock?

opts.a: A feature to lock S3 Glacier vaults from being deleted for cost savings
opts.b: A WORM compliance feature that allows you to lock a vault policy to enforce regulatory retention controls that cannot be changed
opts.c: A feature to encrypt Glacier archives with customer keys
opts.d: A feature to prevent unauthorized vault creation

exp.a: Incorrect. Vault Lock is about policy enforcement, not just deletion prevention.
exp.b: Correct. Glacier Vault Lock allows you to enforce compliance controls by locking a vault policy (WORM). Once locked, the policy can never be changed or deleted.
exp.c: Incorrect. Encryption is separate from Vault Lock.
exp.d: Incorrect. Vault Lock applies to existing vaults, not vault creation.

q: What is the maximum metadata size (user-defined + system metadata) that can be attached to an S3 object?

opts.b: 8 KB

exp.a: Correct. The total size of user-defined metadata (all key-value pairs in the x-amz-meta- headers) cannot exceed 2 KB.
exp.b: Incorrect. 8 KB exceeds the metadata size limit.
exp.c: Incorrect. 16 KB exceeds the metadata size limit.
exp.d: Incorrect. 64 KB far exceeds the metadata size limit.

q: What is the maximum length of an S3 object key (object name)?

opts.b: 512 characters

exp.a: Incorrect. The limit is measured in bytes, not just characters.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is 1,024 bytes.
exp.c: Correct. An S3 object key can be up to 1,024 bytes in length (UTF-8 encoded).
exp.d: Incorrect. It's 1,024 bytes, not 1,024 characters (multi-byte UTF-8 characters count as more than 1 byte).

q: What happens when you enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering and an object is not accessed for 30 consecutive days?

opts.b: The object is moved to the Infrequent Access tier automatically
opts.c: The object is moved to Glacier
opts.d: A notification is sent to the bucket owner

exp.a: Incorrect. Intelligent-Tiering does not delete objects.
exp.b: Correct. After 30 consecutive days without access, objects are automatically moved from the Frequent Access tier to the Infrequent Access tier.
exp.c: Incorrect. Objects move to the optional Archive Access tier after 90 days (if configured), not after 30 days.
exp.d: Incorrect. No notification is sent; the transition happens automatically.

q: In S3 Intelligent-Tiering, after how many days of no access are objects moved to the Archive Instant Access tier?

opts.b: 60 days

exp.a: Incorrect. 30 days triggers movement to the Infrequent Access tier.
exp.b: Incorrect. There is no 60-day tier in Intelligent-Tiering.
exp.c: Correct. After 90 consecutive days without access, objects are moved to the Archive Instant Access tier.
exp.d: Incorrect. 180 days is for the optional Deep Archive Access tier.

q: Does S3 Intelligent-Tiering charge retrieval fees?

opts.b: No, there are no retrieval fees but there is a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object
opts.c: Yes, same as Glacier retrieval fees
opts.d: No fees of any kind beyond standard storage

exp.a: Incorrect. There are no retrieval fees in Intelligent-Tiering.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fees. It charges a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object (per 1,000 objects).
exp.c: Incorrect. Intelligent-Tiering does not charge Glacier-style retrieval fees.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a small monitoring/automation fee in addition to storage costs.

q: Which condition key in an S3 bucket policy can be used to restrict uploads to only SSE-KMS encrypted objects?

opts.b: s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption: aws:kms

exp.a: Incorrect. x-amz-acl is for specifying ACL permissions on upload.
exp.b: Correct. Using the condition key s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption with the value aws:kms in a Deny statement enforces that only SSE-KMS encrypted uploads are allowed.
exp.c: Incorrect. x-amz-copy-source specifies the source for copy operations.
exp.d: Incorrect. x-amz-storage-class specifies the storage class, not encryption.

q: What is S3 Bucket Key and what problem does it solve?

opts.a: A master key stored in the bucket for SSE-S3 encryption
opts.b: A bucket-level key that reduces the number of KMS API calls (and cost) when using SSE-KMS
opts.c: A key used to lock bucket configurations
opts.d: A unique identifier for bucket policies

exp.a: Incorrect. SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 automatically, not via Bucket Key.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Bucket Keys reduce the number of requests to AWS KMS by generating a bucket-level key that creates data keys locally, reducing KMS costs by up to 99%.
exp.c: Incorrect. Bucket Key is about encryption cost optimization.
exp.d: Incorrect. Bucket Key is unrelated to policy identifiers.

q: Which S3 Lifecycle action can you NOT perform?

opts.a: Transition objects from Standard to Standard-IA
opts.b: Transition objects from Standard-IA to S3 Standard
opts.c: Transition objects from Standard to Glacier
opts.d: Expire (delete) objects after a certain number of days

exp.a: Incorrect. You CAN transition from Standard to Standard-IA.
exp.b: Correct. Lifecycle rules can only transition objects to lower-cost tiers (waterfall model). You cannot transition from Standard-IA back to Standard using lifecycle rules.
exp.c: Incorrect. You CAN transition from Standard to Glacier.
exp.d: Incorrect. You CAN expire objects using lifecycle rules.

q: What is the minimum number of days an object must be in S3 Standard before it can be transitioned to S3 Standard-IA via a lifecycle rule?

opts.b: 7 days

exp.a: Incorrect. There is a minimum duration constraint.
exp.b: Incorrect. 7 days is not the minimum.
exp.c: Correct. Objects must remain in S3 Standard for at least 30 days before being transitioned to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA via lifecycle rules.
exp.d: Incorrect. 90 days is the minimum duration for Glacier Flexible Retrieval, not the transition constraint from Standard.

q: What is the S3 Lifecycle constraint for transitioning objects from Standard-IA to Glacier classes?

opts.b: Objects must be in Standard-IA for at least 30 days
opts.c: Objects must be in Standard-IA for at least 90 days
opts.d: Objects must be in Standard-IA for at least 180 days

exp.a: Incorrect. There is a minimum duration constraint for IA classes.
exp.b: Correct. Objects must remain in Standard-IA for at least 30 days (matching the minimum storage duration charge) before transitioning to a Glacier class.
exp.c: Incorrect. 90 days is not the constraint for this transition.
exp.d: Incorrect. 180 days is the minimum storage for Glacier Deep Archive, not this transition.

q: What is the purpose of S3 Access Analyzer for S3?

opts.a: To analyze storage costs and recommend savings
opts.b: To identify S3 buckets that are shared with external entities (outside your account/organization)
opts.c: To compress objects for better performance
opts.d: To encrypt objects that are unencrypted

exp.a: Incorrect. Cost analysis is done by S3 Storage Lens or Cost Explorer.
exp.b: Correct. IAM Access Analyzer for S3 monitors bucket policies and ACLs to identify buckets accessible by external entities outside your account or AWS Organization.
exp.c: Incorrect. Access Analyzer does not compress objects.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access Analyzer does not encrypt objects.

q: Which S3 notification delivery mechanism provides the most flexibility for routing events to multiple targets?

opts.b: SQS Queue

exp.a: Incorrect. SNS can fan out to multiple subscribers but has fewer built-in integrations than EventBridge.
exp.b: Incorrect. SQS is a single queue destination.
exp.c: Incorrect. Lambda is a single function destination.
exp.d: Correct. Amazon EventBridge provides the most flexibility with 18+ AWS service targets, advanced filtering, multiple destinations, archiving, replay, and integration with third-party SaaS.

q: What is the S3 Multi-Region Access Point?

opts.a: A feature to access S3 from multiple VPCs in the same region
opts.b: A global endpoint that routes S3 requests to the closest bucket replica based on latency for active-active replication
opts.c: A feature that creates multiple copies of a bucket in the same region
opts.d: A DNS alias for a single S3 bucket

exp.a: Incorrect. VPC access is handled by VPC endpoints.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Multi-Region Access Points provide a global endpoint that routes requests to the nearest replicated bucket based on network latency, enabling active-active architectures.
exp.c: Incorrect. Multi-Region implies multiple regions, not same region copies.
exp.d: Incorrect. It routes to multiple buckets across regions, not just a DNS alias for one bucket.

q: What failover capability does S3 Multi-Region Access Point provide?

opts.b: Automatic failover only
opts.c: Active-active routing with the ability to control failover (active-passive) between regions

exp.a: Incorrect. Multi-Region Access Points support failover.
exp.b: Incorrect. You can manually control failover routing, not just automatic.
exp.c: Correct. S3 Multi-Region Access Points support both active-active routing and manual failover control to shift traffic between regions.
exp.d: Incorrect. You can control failover at any time, not just during outages.

q: What is the key difference between S3 Access Points and S3 Multi-Region Access Points?

opts.a: Access Points are for encryption; Multi-Region Access Points are for replication
opts.b: Access Points simplify per-application access to a single bucket; Multi-Region Access Points route requests across multiple buckets in different regions
opts.c: They are the same feature with different names
opts.d: Access Points are only for VPC access; Multi-Region Access Points are for internet access

exp.a: Incorrect. Neither is specifically for encryption or replication alone.
exp.b: Correct. Access Points create named endpoints with unique policies for a single bucket. Multi-Region Access Points create a global endpoint routing to multiple replicated buckets across regions.
exp.c: Incorrect. They are different features with different purposes.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access Points can be internet-facing or VPC-restricted. Multi-Region Access Points route globally.

q: What is the maximum number of S3 Access Points per AWS account per region by default?

exp.a: Incorrect. The default limit is much higher.
exp.b: Incorrect. 1,000 is the limit for buckets, not access points.
exp.c: Correct. By default, you can create up to 10,000 Access Points per AWS account per region.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a default limit of 10,000.

q: When using S3 Object Lock with a Legal Hold, what is required to remove the hold?

opts.b: The s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission
opts.d: The retention period must expire first

exp.a: Incorrect. Root access is not specifically required; any user with the right permission can remove it.
exp.b: Correct. A user with the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission can place or remove a Legal Hold at any time, regardless of retention settings.
exp.c: Incorrect. MFA is not required to remove Legal Hold (MFA Delete is a different feature).
exp.d: Incorrect. Legal Hold is independent of retention periods and can be removed anytime by authorized users.

q: What is the S3 Storage Class for data that can be easily recreated and requires the lowest cost?

opts.b: S3 One Zone-IA
opts.d: S3 Reduced Redundancy Storage (RRS) - deprecated, so S3 One Zone-IA

exp.a: Incorrect. Standard-IA replicates across 3+ AZs and costs more than One Zone-IA.
exp.b: Correct. S3 One Zone-IA is ideal for data that can be recreated because it stores data in a single AZ at lower cost. If the AZ is destroyed, the data is lost.
exp.c: Incorrect. Glacier Deep Archive is for data that cannot be easily recreated and needs long-term retention.
exp.d: Incorrect. RRS is deprecated; One Zone-IA is the appropriate choice for re-creatable data.

q: What is the availability SLA for S3 One Zone-IA?

exp.a: Incorrect. 99.99% is for S3 Standard.
exp.b: Incorrect. 99.9% is for S3 Standard-IA.
exp.c: Correct. S3 One Zone-IA has an availability SLA of 99.5% since data is in a single AZ.
exp.d: Incorrect. 99% is lower than the actual SLA for One Zone-IA.

q: Which S3 feature allows you to create a point-in-time snapshot of your bucket for compliance purposes?

opts.b: S3 Inventory combined with S3 Batch Operations
opts.d: S3 does not support native point-in-time snapshots; you use versioning for object-level recovery

exp.a: Incorrect. Versioning keeps versions but is not a point-in-time snapshot.
exp.b: Incorrect. Inventory reports contents but doesn't create a restorable snapshot.
exp.c: Incorrect. Replication copies objects to another bucket but is not a snapshot.
exp.d: Correct. S3 does not have a native point-in-time snapshot feature like EBS. Versioning provides object-level version history for recovery.

q: How does S3 handle concurrent PUT requests to the same object key?

opts.a: It queues them and processes sequentially
opts.b: The last write wins (last writer wins semantics)
opts.c: It returns an error for the second PUT
opts.d: It creates multiple versions automatically even without versioning

exp.a: Incorrect. S3 does not queue concurrent writes.
exp.b: Correct. With concurrent PUTs to the same key (without versioning), S3 uses last-writer-wins semantics based on the timestamp received by S3.
exp.c: Incorrect. Both PUTs succeed but the last one wins.
exp.d: Incorrect. Without versioning enabled, only one version exists and the last write overwrites.

q: What is S3 Byte-Range Fetches?

opts.a: A feature to upload objects in byte ranges
opts.b: The ability to GET specific byte ranges of an object using the Range HTTP header for parallel downloads or partial retrieval
opts.c: A feature to delete specific bytes from an object
opts.d: A feature to encrypt only specific bytes of an object

exp.a: Incorrect. Byte-range fetches are for downloads, not uploads (multipart is for uploads).
exp.b: Correct. S3 supports byte-range fetches using the Range HTTP header, allowing parallel downloads of different parts of an object or retrieval of only specific portions.
exp.c: Incorrect. You cannot delete specific bytes; S3 objects are immutable.
exp.d: Incorrect. Encryption applies to the entire object.

q: Which S3 feature provides automatic cost optimization by analyzing incomplete multipart uploads?

opts.b: S3 Lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads

exp.a: Incorrect. Storage Lens provides metrics but doesn't automatically clean up.
exp.b: Correct. You can configure a lifecycle rule to automatically abort incomplete multipart uploads after a specified number of days, preventing storage charges for orphaned parts.
exp.c: Incorrect. Intelligent-Tiering manages storage classes, not incomplete uploads.
exp.d: Incorrect. Analytics provides access pattern analysis, not cleanup of incomplete uploads.

q: Which AWS service can be used to migrate large datasets from on-premises to S3 offline?

opts.b: AWS Snow Family (Snowball/Snowmobile)

exp.a: Incorrect. DataSync transfers data over the network (online), not offline.
exp.b: Correct. AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge, Snowcone, Snowmobile) enables offline/physical data migration of large datasets to S3.
exp.c: Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration speeds up online transfers, not offline.
exp.d: Incorrect. Direct Connect is a dedicated network connection (online).

q: What is the storage capacity of a single AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device?

opts.b: 42 TB

exp.a: Incorrect. 8 TB is the capacity of Snowcone.
exp.b: Incorrect. 42 TB was for the older Snowball (now deprecated).
exp.c: Correct. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized provides 80 TB of usable storage.
exp.d: Incorrect. 100 PB is the capacity of Snowmobile.

q: What is the purpose of S3 Inventory reports in the context of replication?

opts.b: To audit and identify objects that failed to replicate, enabling S3 Batch Replication to fix them

exp.a: Incorrect. Inventory does not replace replication.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Inventory can include replication status, helping identify objects that failed replication. You can then use S3 Batch Replication to replicate those failed objects.
exp.c: Incorrect. Inventory reports do not speed up replication.
exp.d: Incorrect. Inventory does not handle encryption.

q: What is the maximum number of lifecycle rules per S3 bucket?

exp.a: Incorrect. You can have more than 100 lifecycle rules.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is higher than 500.
exp.c: Correct. You can configure up to 1,000 lifecycle rules per S3 bucket.
exp.d: Incorrect. There is a limit of 1,000 lifecycle rules.

q: When using S3 Select with a CSV file, which of the following SQL operations is NOT supported?

opts.b: JOIN between two objects

exp.a: Incorrect. SELECT with WHERE is supported in S3 Select.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Select does not support JOIN operations. It can only query a single object at a time.
exp.c: Incorrect. LIMIT is supported in S3 Select.
exp.d: Incorrect. Aggregate functions are supported in S3 Select.

q: What file formats does S3 Select support?

opts.b: Only CSV and JSON

exp.a: Correct. S3 Select supports CSV, JSON, and Apache Parquet file formats.
exp.b: Incorrect. Apache Parquet is also supported.
exp.c: Incorrect. ORC is supported by Athena but not by S3 Select.
exp.d: Incorrect. Only CSV, JSON, and Parquet are supported.

q: What is the difference between S3 Select and Amazon Athena?

opts.a: S3 Select is for querying a single object; Athena can query across multiple objects/files with full SQL support
opts.b: They are identical services
opts.c: Athena can only query Parquet files; S3 Select supports all formats
opts.d: S3 Select requires a database schema; Athena is schema-less

exp.a: Correct. S3 Select performs simple SQL on a single object. Athena is a serverless query engine supporting full ANSI SQL across multiple objects, partitions, and formats.
exp.b: Incorrect. They are different services with different capabilities.
exp.c: Incorrect. Athena supports many formats including CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, Avro.
exp.d: Incorrect. Athena requires schema definition in the Glue Data Catalog; S3 Select is simpler.

q: What is S3 Object Ownership and what change was made in April 2023?

opts.a: A feature to transfer bucket ownership; no changes were made
opts.b: A setting that controls whether ACLs are enabled; as of April 2023 new buckets have ACLs disabled by default (BucketOwnerEnforced)
opts.c: A feature that allows multiple accounts to own the same object
opts.d: A feature that encrypts objects with owner-specific keys

exp.a: Incorrect. Object Ownership doesn't transfer bucket ownership.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Object Ownership controls ACL behavior. Since April 2023, new buckets default to BucketOwnerEnforced (ACLs disabled), making the bucket owner the automatic owner of all objects.
exp.c: Incorrect. Each object has a single owner.
exp.d: Incorrect. Object Ownership is about access control, not encryption.

q: What is the S3 pricing model for data transfer?

opts.a: Data transfer IN and OUT are both free
opts.b: Data transfer IN is free; data transfer OUT to the internet is charged per GB
opts.c: Data transfer IN is charged; OUT is free
opts.d: Both IN and OUT are charged per GB

exp.a: Incorrect. Data transfer OUT is not free.
exp.b: Correct. Data transfer INTO S3 from the internet is free. Data transfer OUT from S3 to the internet is charged per GB (with the first 100 GB/month free for all AWS services combined since Dec 2021).
exp.c: Incorrect. Data transfer IN is free.
exp.d: Incorrect. Only data transfer OUT is charged.

q: What is the free tier for S3 data transfer OUT to the internet per month?

opts.b: 15 GB

exp.a: Incorrect. The free tier was expanded from 1 GB.
exp.b: Incorrect. 15 GB is not the current free tier for data transfer out.
exp.c: Correct. As of December 2021, AWS provides 100 GB of free data transfer out per month (shared across all AWS services).
exp.d: Incorrect. 1 TB exceeds the free tier.

q: Which S3 feature can prevent accidental bucket deletion?

opts.b: S3 Object Lock
opts.c: A bucket policy that denies s3:DeleteBucket or using an SCP (Service Control Policy)

exp.a: Incorrect. Versioning protects objects, not the bucket itself from deletion.
exp.b: Incorrect. Object Lock protects objects from deletion, not the bucket.
exp.c: Correct. A bucket policy denying s3:DeleteBucket or an SCP in AWS Organizations can prevent accidental bucket deletion. Note: a bucket must be empty to be deleted.
exp.d: Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration is for upload speed, not deletion protection.

q: Can you change the region of an existing S3 bucket?

opts.a: Yes, using the AWS CLI migrate command
opts.b: Yes, by updating the bucket configuration
opts.c: No, you must create a new bucket in the desired region and copy/replicate data

exp.a: Incorrect. There is no migrate command to change a bucket's region.
exp.b: Incorrect. The region of a bucket cannot be changed after creation.
exp.c: Correct. Once a bucket is created in a region, it cannot be moved. You must create a new bucket in the target region and use CRR, DataSync, or CLI copy to transfer data.
exp.d: Incorrect. Even AWS Support cannot change a bucket's region.

q: What is the purpose of S3 Access Grants?

opts.a: To grant temporary access to S3 via presigned URLs
opts.b: To map identities from corporate directories to S3 dataset permissions at scale, integrating with IAM Identity Center
opts.c: To create public access grants for open datasets

exp.a: Incorrect. Presigned URLs are different from Access Grants.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Access Grants provide a simplified way to grant access to S3 data at scale by mapping corporate identities (from IAM Identity Center/directory) to dataset-level permissions.
exp.c: Incorrect. Access Grants are not for making data public.
exp.d: Incorrect. Access Grants work beyond just cross-account scenarios.

q: Which AWS service can trigger a Lambda function when a new object is uploaded to S3 for image processing?

opts.b: S3 Event Notifications

exp.a: Incorrect. CloudWatch monitors metrics/logs but doesn't directly trigger Lambda from S3 uploads.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Event Notifications can directly invoke a Lambda function on s3:ObjectCreated events for real-time processing like image resizing.
exp.c: Incorrect. Step Functions orchestrate workflows but need to be triggered; they don't natively listen to S3 events directly (EventBridge can bridge this).
exp.d: Incorrect. AWS Batch is for batch computing jobs, not event-driven S3 processing.

q: What is the S3 notification delivery guarantee when using EventBridge vs. traditional S3 event notifications (SNS/SQS/Lambda)?

opts.b: EventBridge provides at-least-once delivery with better reliability; traditional notifications deliver at-least-once but may miss events in rare cases
opts.c: Traditional notifications are more reliable than EventBridge

exp.a: Incorrect. Neither guarantees exactly-once delivery.
exp.b: Correct. EventBridge provides at-least-once delivery with better reliability and doesn't require manual configuration of permissions on the target. Traditional S3 notifications also provide at-least-once but EventBridge offers more advanced capabilities.
exp.c: Incorrect. EventBridge is generally more reliable and feature-rich.
exp.d: Incorrect. Both provide at-least-once delivery guarantees.

q: What is S3 Storage Class Analysis and how long does it take to provide actionable recommendations?

opts.b: Observes access patterns for 24-48 hours before recommending
opts.c: Observes access patterns for 30 days or more before providing transition recommendations
opts.d: Only available via AWS Support request

exp.a: Incorrect. It needs time to observe access patterns.
exp.b: Incorrect. 24-48 hours is insufficient for meaningful analysis.
exp.c: Correct. S3 Storage Class Analysis observes access patterns for 30 days or more before providing recommendations on when to transition objects to IA storage classes.
exp.d: Incorrect. It's a self-service feature enabled in the S3 console.

q: What is the maximum size of a bucket policy in Amazon S3?

opts.b: 10 KB

exp.a: Incorrect. 2 KB is too small for most bucket policies.
exp.b: Incorrect. The limit is larger than 10 KB.
exp.c: Correct. An S3 bucket policy can be up to 20 KB in size.
exp.d: Incorrect. 64 KB exceeds the bucket policy size limit.

q: When configuring S3 Cross-Region Replication, which IAM entity does S3 assume to perform replication?

opts.b: An IAM Role with permissions to read from source and write to destination
opts.d: An S3 service-linked role that is automatically created

exp.a: Incorrect. S3 does not use IAM user credentials for replication.
exp.b: Correct. You must create an IAM Role that S3 assumes to replicate objects. This role needs GetObject/GetObjectVersion on source and PutObject/ReplicateObject on destination.
exp.c: Incorrect. Root account is not used for service operations.
exp.d: Incorrect. The replication role is not automatically created; you must create and configure it.

q: What is the purpose of S3 Batch Replication?

opts.b: To replicate existing objects that were uploaded before replication was enabled, or objects that previously failed to replicate
opts.c: To replicate objects in batch every 24 hours
opts.d: To replicate delete markers in bulk

exp.a: Incorrect. Batch Replication is not about speed for new objects.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Batch Replication is used to replicate existing objects, objects that failed replication, or objects replicated under a prior rule.
exp.c: Incorrect. Batch Replication is on-demand, not scheduled every 24 hours.
exp.d: Incorrect. Batch Replication handles objects, not specifically delete markers.

q: Which S3 feature helps comply with data residency requirements by ensuring data stays within a specific AWS Region?

opts.b: S3 bucket region selection at creation time

exp.a: Incorrect. CRR explicitly moves data to another region, which would violate data residency.
exp.b: Correct. When you create an S3 bucket, you choose a specific AWS Region. Data never leaves that region unless you explicitly configure replication or transfer it.
exp.c: Incorrect. Transfer Acceleration routes through edge locations but data is still stored in the bucket's region.
exp.d: Incorrect. Intelligent-Tiering manages storage classes within the same region.

q: What is S3 Express One Zone storage class designed for?

opts.b: Single-digit millisecond latency for performance-intensive applications with data in a single Availability Zone

exp.a: Incorrect. Express One Zone is for high-performance, not archival.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Express One Zone is designed for single-digit millisecond latency, up to 10x faster than S3 Standard, for latency-sensitive workloads with data stored in a single AZ.
exp.c: Incorrect. It's single-zone, not multi-region.
exp.d: Incorrect. It's a performance-optimized class, not a cost-optimized IA class.

q: What type of bucket does S3 Express One Zone use?

opts.b: Directory bucket

exp.a: Incorrect. General purpose buckets are for all other S3 storage classes.
exp.b: Correct. S3 Express One Zone uses a new bucket type called Directory Buckets, which have a different naming convention and API behavior.
exp.c: Incorrect. There is no archive bucket type.
exp.d: Incorrect. It requires a completely new directory bucket type.

q: What is the ListObjectsV2 pagination limit for the maximum number of keys returned per request?

exp.a: Incorrect. The default/max per page is higher than 100.
exp.b: Incorrect. The maximum is 1,000, not 500.
exp.c: Correct. ListObjectsV2 returns up to 1,000 keys per request. For more keys, you must paginate using the ContinuationToken.
exp.d: Incorrect. 10,000 exceeds the single-request limit.

q: What happens to S3 storage costs when versioning is enabled and objects are frequently updated?

opts.a: Costs remain the same since only the latest version is stored
opts.b: Costs increase because all versions are stored and you pay for the total storage of all versions
opts.c: Costs decrease because older versions are compressed
opts.d: Only the last 5 versions are retained

exp.a: Incorrect. All versions are stored, not just the latest.
exp.b: Correct. With versioning enabled, every version of every object is retained and you are charged for the storage of ALL versions. This can significantly increase costs for frequently updated objects.
exp.c: Incorrect. Older versions are not compressed; they are stored as full objects.
exp.d: Incorrect. All versions are retained unless explicitly deleted or managed by lifecycle rules.

q: How can you reduce costs when using versioning by removing old versions?

opts.a: Disable versioning to delete all old versions
opts.b: Use a lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration to delete noncurrent versions after a specified number of days
opts.c: Old versions are automatically deleted after 30 days
opts.d: Contact AWS Support to purge old versions

exp.a: Incorrect. Disabling (suspending) versioning does not delete existing old versions.
exp.b: Correct. A lifecycle rule with NoncurrentVersionExpiration automatically deletes noncurrent object versions after a configured number of days.
exp.c: Incorrect. Old versions are never automatically deleted without an explicit lifecycle rule.
exp.d: Incorrect. This is self-service via lifecycle rules.

q: What is the NoncurrentVersionTransition action in S3 Lifecycle rules?

opts.a: Transitioning current versions to a cheaper class
opts.b: Transitioning noncurrent (old) versions to a cheaper storage class like Glacier before eventually expiring them
opts.d: Moving noncurrent versions to another bucket

exp.a: Incorrect. Current version transitions use the Transition action, not NoncurrentVersionTransition.
exp.b: Correct. NoncurrentVersionTransition moves noncurrent versions to cheaper storage classes (e.g., Standard-IA, Glacier) after a specified number of days since becoming noncurrent.
exp.c: Incorrect. Deletion is handled by NoncurrentVersionExpiration.
exp.d: Incorrect. Lifecycle rules don't move objects to another bucket.

q: What is the S3 feature that enables you to enforce specific conditions before allowing cross-account access to a bucket?

opts.b: Bucket Policy with Principal and Condition elements

exp.a: Incorrect. ACLs provide basic permissions but lack fine-grained conditions.
exp.b: Correct. Bucket policies support Principal (to specify the external account/role) and Condition elements (to enforce MFA, IP range, VPC endpoint, encryption, etc.) for cross-account access control.
exp.c: Incorrect. Versioning manages object versions, not access control.
exp.d: Incorrect. Storage Lens provides metrics, not access control.
